subject: Architecture
title: Wind Tunnels Between Skyscrapers
description: A quick win: understand Wind Tunnels Between Skyscrapers.

hook.text: Some city streets are so windy that pedestrians get knocked off their feet — buildings create invisible tunnels.

buildup.text: Tall buildings funnel wind into narrow gaps between them — accelerating airflow to dangerous speeds.

discovery.text: The Venturi effect squeezes air between towers, doubling or tripling wind speed at street level.

twist.text: Leeds' Bridgewater Place created winds so strong that a truck was blown over, killing a pedestrian in 2011.

climax.text: Cities now require wind studies before approving tall buildings — preventing dangerous street-level gusts.

punchline.text: Buildings don't just block wind. They weaponize it.

quiz.question: What physical principle causes wind acceleration between tall buildings?
options: The Coriolis effect deflecting airflow at ground level
The Venturi effect squeezing air through narrow gaps
Thermal convection pulling cold air down building facades

details.summary: Tall buildings can accelerate street-level winds to dangerous speeds through the Venturi effect — where wind squeezes between buildings and speeds up. Pedestrians have been knocked down and injured in wind corridors created by poorly spaced towers in cities like London, Chicago, and Hong Kong.
details.whyItMatters: Wind comfort is an invisible dimension of urban design. Buildings that look spectacular in renderings can create miserable, even dangerous, street conditions if their effect on wind patterns isn't modeled during design.
takeaways: Tall buildings can accelerate wind to dangerous street-level speeds
The Venturi effect squeezes and accelerates wind between towers
Pedestrians have been injured by wind corridors between buildings

faq.question: How do buildings create wind tunnels?
faq.answer: When wind hits a tall building, it deflects downward and around the sides. If another building is nearby, the gap between them acts like a nozzle, compressing the air and increasing its speed dramatically. This downwash effect is worst at the base of very tall, flat-faced buildings.

faq.question: Can wind tunnel effects be prevented?
faq.answer: Yes. Setbacks at ground level, canopies, podium bases, rounded building corners, porous facades, and strategic vegetation can all reduce wind acceleration. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling during design can identify and solve wind problems before buildings are constructed.
